Part I — Knowledge Base (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Knowledge Base (Session 20)
Topic: Bhog (Food Offerings) — Who Can Actually Feed a Devta, and Why Household Offerings Often Feed Pitrus Instead

Sour ce: Bhaiya's live satsang session (video transcript, ~98 min), deliver ed during an ongoing hawan. Opens with a short comparative teaching on Krishna bhakti versus Ram bhakti, then moves into the session's main topic: the astral hierar chy of Bhagwan/Devta/Doot, why most household food offerings (bhog) never actually r each the intended deity , and what a devotee should do instead — followed by extensive live sangat Q&A. Purpose: Chatbot knowledge — English version.
1. EVER YTHING HAPPENS BY PRABHU'S WILL, NOT OUR OWN

The session opens with a gr ounding r eminder: whatever is happening, however it's happening, is happening entir ely by Prabhu's (God's) will — never purely by one's own choice or effort. Those who have lived long enough (past roughly 50) tend to intuitively accept "hoi so wahi jo Ram rachi rakha" (whatever happens is what Ram has already written); younger people often resist this, believing "I can do anything myself." Simply being pr esent to hear a given teaching is itself framed as the first sign that Prabhu wanted that specific listener to hear it.
2. KRISHNA BHAKTI VS. RAM BHAKTI — A PRACTICAL COMPARISON

A devotee of Bhagwan Krishna, practically speaking, often r eceives comfort quickly: material wealth, a comfortable lifestyle, business success, plenty to eat, family harmony at home. But this comes with a counterweight: such a devotee often lacks maan-pratishtha (dignity/r espect) — they may be blamed or insulted by others despite their prosperity , sometimes even by their own family , and can end up having to live somewhat apart from their community's approval, however wealthy they've become. A devotee of Bhagwan Ram, by contrast, is first sent thr ough a period of "vanvas" (exile/hardship) — not necessarily 14 literal years, but a proportional hardship period (which the session illustrates as ranging from as little as six months up to roughly two years, depending on the devotee's own grahan shakti/receptivity and karma). Once this vanvas period genuinely completes, the devotee r eceives "raj yog" (a kingship-like elevation) — respect that lasts across generations, a family name that's never tarnished, and children who are recognized and spoken well of specifically because of that name. The stated r eason for this difference: Bhagwan Krishna himself carried one specific flaw in his own life — despite being "Jagat Guru" (teacher of the whole world), he could not fully guide or correct his own son, and his own kingdom, Dwarka, was ultimately destroyed. A devotee who takes on Krishna's tattva may inherit an echo of this same specific pattern — comfort and prosperity , but a persistent gap in being fully honored or listened to by one's closest circle. This comparison is offer ed as a practical, factual observation, not as a claim that Ram is "better than" Krishna — Bhaiya is explicit that Krishna is Krishna, a full Bhagwan in his own right, and this is not meant to diminish that.
3. NOT EVERY OUTCOME IS SOLELY "YOUR OWN DOING" — LEARN, DON'T OVER-OWN

Illustrative example: even Mata Sita, upon whom Maya herself bows, was made to cr oss the Lakshman Rekha by Maya's own dir ect intervention in that moment — yet the world still says "you did it, you should have known better , you're responsible." The teaching drawn fr om this: when something goes wr ong due to cir cumstances genuinely beyond your contr ol, learn fr om it ("it happened thr ough me, but it won't r epeat") without permanently claiming full personal blame or responsibility for it — because if you claim full responsibility for the bad, you'll also end up wrongly claiming full responsibility for the good, and living entirely inside that self-focused framework leads to unnecessary despair . Even Bhagwan Krishna, asked how he holds up Govardhan Parvat on a single finger , would say "I didn't do it — Prabhu did it thr ough me," not personally claim the feat. Life is compared to a movie — not something to hold too close or push too far away emotionally .
4. THE ASTRAL HIERARCHY — BHAGWAN, DEVTA, AND DOOT

Three distinct categories exist: Bhagwan (God) — pr esent absolutely everywher e (sarvatra), transcendent; Devta — what Bhagwan becomes when taking on a saakar (manifest, form-based) form, tied to a specific sour ce of energy; and Doot — messengers/agents who work under and carry out a devta's will. Krishna, Hanuman Ji Maharaj, Bhagwan Shiv , and other worshipped figur es all simultaneously exist in all thr ee forms — as Bhagwan, as Devta, and as Doot — this hierarchy applies universally across deities, even though it's rarely explicitly understood by ordinary devotees. A being that is truly Bhagwan (pr esent everywher e, formless in this sense) literally cannot "eat" a physical food offering — only a saakar (manifest) form, such as a devta's specific present ener gy , or an actual physical being, can receive an of fering at all. If a devotee wants their bhog to genuinely r each the devta, that devta's pr esence must first genuinely exist wherever the offering is being made — it's not automatic.
5. WHY MOST HOUSEHOLD BHOG NEVER REACHES THE ACTUAL DEVTA

When a person's own sankalp shakti (willpower/spiritual capacity) and dimension ar e weak, and no r eal pr otection is in place, an offering intended for a devta doesn't r each that devta at all — instead, any nearby wandering entity (a preta/spirit) can simply claim the identity being invoked ("I am Krishna," "I am Kanha") and start consuming the daily of fering, ef fectively taking up residence near the household idol (e.g., a Laddu Gopal murti). This arrangement is self-r einfor cing: daily feeding builds a r eal, gr owing connection and str ength for that entity over time, since a genuine (if illegitimate) ener getic link forms through the repeated of fering. The entity will try to "pr ove its existence" thr ough small material favors — minor coincidences, a wished-for phone appearing, and similar modest wins — but it categorically CANNOT change the person's actual destiny , since it remains bound to its own limited capacity (illustrated with the analogy of a road roller: however much fuel/investment you put into it, it will never become an airplane — it can only ever do what a road roller does). The true Bhagwan Krishna is not tr oubled or threatened by this substitution, and does not intervene to corr ect it — both the sincere devotee and the impostor entity are, in this framework, equally "his children," so there's no dif ferential concern shown between them.
6. WHY THIS MATTERS SO MUCH — AND WHO CAN ACTUALLY OFFER BHOG

This entire dynamic is exactly why drishti (third-eye/spiritual sight) matters so much: without it, a devotee has no way to know whether their offering is genuinely r eaching the intended devta or being inter cepted by something else entir ely .

Most small, informally-built neighborhood temples (put together quickly by a handful of people pooling money , with a hurried pran-pratishtha cer emony) ar e, in this framework, populated mostly by pr etas rather than genuine devtas — by contrast, siddh mandirs (temples established thr ough a gr eat saint's genuine tapasya) do carry authentic devta pr esence. Only very advanced, r ealized saints — whose own tap-shakti (accumulated spiritual power) has genuinely manifested a devta in physical form, and whose own energy matches that devta's energy exactly — ar e actually capable of offering bhog dir ectly (the session's examples: Haridas Ji and Ramdas Ji, gurus associated with Tansen's lineage). This is also the underlying r eason some South Indian temple traditions r estrict bhog offerings inside the garbha griha (inner sanctum) to trained pandits alone — ordinary devotees generally lack the capacity for this specific act.
7. PRACTICAL GUIDANCE — WHAT ORDINARY DEVOTEES SHOULD ACTUALLY DO

Direct recommendation: ordinary devotees should NOT perform bhog (food offerings) at home. Instead, of fering a deepak (a lamp, via agni/fire) is presented as squarely within an ordinary devotee's real authority and capacity — this is the safer , appr opriate practice. If a devotee wants to dedicate a bhog-style offering safely , they can do so via "sakshi maan ke" (tr eating a trusted figur e as witness) thr ough Hanuman Ji Maharaj specifically — Bhaiya explains that his own sookshma sharir (subtle body) carries the authority and responsibility to relay such dedications directly to his own Gurudev , Hanuman Ji Maharaj, who then passes it onward (e.g., to Bholenath) as appropriate. This works specifically because it goes thr ough the Guru with genuine humility ("sirodhari karke" — carrying the Guru "on one's head"). Bhaiya states he personally never performs bhog himself, despite people telling him he could simply "eat" what's offer ed — his own stated reason: he still carries kaam, krodh, lobh, mad, moh, matsar (desire, anger , greed, pride, attachment, envy) like any person, and doesn't want his own inner fluctuations to risk interfering with properly relaying a devotee's true intention.
8. WHY PITRUS SPECIFICALLY END UP "EATING" HOUSEHOLD OFFERINGS

A specific, common trap: if a devotee names a deceased family member (a pitru) dir ectly while making an offering — even a small, once-a-year offering on a death anniversary — the pitru gets first claim on that offering, ahead of any genuine devta , regardless of what deity's name is also invoked. Pitrus have a kind of "default jurisdiction" within their own family's home. Regularly feeding a pitru this way builds it into a powerful, entr enched presence ("raja"/king) within that home. When the devotee later prays sincerely at a genuinely powerful temple and devta doots are dispatched to help, those doots will r efuse to enter and act inside a home wher e a str ong pitru pr esence is alr eady established — they follow strict pr otocol and won't for ce their way past it , even though they're often described as being under a devta as senior as Bhagwan Shiv . This is the likely explanation for a specific, common pattern many people notice without understanding it: feeling wonderful, light, and clear after visiting a temple, only to feel heavy , uneasy , or discomforted again almost immediately upon r eturning home.
9. THE PHYSICAL SYMPTOM PATTERN LINKED TO HOUSEHOLD PITRU PRESENCE

A specific, repeatedly observed symptom pattern in households with an entr enched pitru: women in particular tend to develop migrating, unexplained body pain — joint or muscle discomfort that cir culates fr om one part of the body to another over time (back one day , arm the next, and so on) , without any clear medical explanation. The presence of this

specific "traveling pain" pattern is tr eated as a meaningful diagnostic sign of pitru involvement, not just an ordinary health complaint. A well-fed pitru may occasionally allow a small number of favorable outcomes to occur (a handful of "lucky wins" out of many hopes) — and will keep reminding the devotee of exactly those wins to sustain their faith and continued feeding, even while overall destiny doesn't meaningfully change. Households with an entr enched pitru or negativity ar e also unlikely to ever produce someone with genuine drishti — but they may instead produce people who go into apparent trance/possession displays, claiming a devi or devta has entered their body . Bhaiya offers a lighthearted diagnostic for this: ask the "possessed" person an unr elated factual question (e.g., a chemistry formula) — a genuine devta wouldn't need or want to perform this kind of theatrical display in the first place.
10. WHAT TO ACTUALLY DO ABOUT AN ONGOING FAMILY OFFERING PRACTICE

If a family alr eady has an established practice of yearly food offerings tied to a deceased r elative (e.g., feeding a cow on a death anniversary), the guidance is not to stop the practice itself, but to change HOW it's dedicated: don't invoke the deceased r elative's name dir ectly — dedicate the same offering to the family's Kul Devta (clan deity) instead. The reasoning given: devtas ar e always "givers"; pitrus ar e never "givers." If other family members (a mother , mother -in-law) ar e unwilling to change a long-standing pitru-offering habit, the advice is not to for ce them — a devotee's own corrected practice is described as suf ficient to protect their own children/direct family line going forward, even if older relatives continue their existing habits. A related, gentler note on continuous mantra jaap that "slips out" involuntarily (e.g., during a period of ritual impurity such as sutak, when formal dedication isn't appr opriate): it's fine to continue quietly r eciting the mantra itself — simply don't formally "dedicate" or "offer" it as bhog during that specific period.
1 1. CONSISTENCY OF MANTRA — DON'T SWITCH BY SEASON OR FESTIVAL

A direct teaching in r esponse to a question about Sawan vrat and mantra practice: don't switch mantras according to season or festival (e.g., "Om Namah Shivaya" during Sawan, "Om Hreem Kleem Chamundaya Vichche" during Navratri, "Om Gan Ganapataye Namah" for Ganesh Chaturthi). A devta is described as far too discerning to be won over by such occasional, opportunistic devotion — they notice a devotee who is only "loyal" to them once or twice a year . The analogy given: no one r espects a carpenter who does carpentry only near a carpenter's shop, then switches to blacksmithing near a blacksmith, then flour -milling near a mill — everyone r ecognizes this as unr eliable and roundabout ("dhokhla aadmi"). Instead, a devotee should stick to ONE consistent mantra and build r eal mastery/value in it over time — that same single mantra, offer ed consistently , is fully sufficient to pr esent to any devta on any occasion , since consistent devotion itself is what accumulates real spiritual value, not switching mantras to match the calendar . Vrat (fasting observances) tied to specific days should only be undertaken by someone whose aura is clean of active negativity or pitru dosha — if either is present, undertaking a vrat risks trapping the practitioner further rather than helping them, and should be avoided until that underlying issue is addressed.
12. ON WOMEN'S PARTICIPATION IN VRAT AND WORSHIP

Women ar e directly encouraged to observe Hanuman Ji vrats on Tuesdays or Saturdays — described plainly as legitimate and valuable ("the r eal worship of Hanuman Ji Maharaj is done by women"). The same caveat applies as above: this should be avoided specifically if active negativity or pitru dosha is present in that person's aura at the time.
QUICK RULES SUMMARY

1. Everything happens by Prabhu's will, not purely by one's own ef fort or choice — simply being present to receive a specific teaching is itself framed as significant. 2. Krishna bhakti tends to bring quick material comfort but often lacks lasting maan-pratishtha (respect); Ram bhakti requires an initial hardship period (vanvas) but yields generational raj yog and untarnished family respect afterward — this reflects each deity's own life pattern, not a ranking of one over the other . 3. Don't fully claim personal responsibility for either bad or good outcomes that were genuinely shaped by forces beyond your control (as with Mata Sita and the Lakshman Rekha) — learn from mistakes without collapsing into total self-blame. 4. The astral hierarchy is Bhagwan (omnipresent, formless) → Devta (a manifest form tied to a real ener gy source) → Doot (messenger/agent) — the same deity exists in all three forms simultaneously . 5. A truly omnipresent Bhagwan cannot literally "eat" a physical bhog of fering — only a genuinely present, manifest (saakar) entity can receive one, and that presence isn't automatic just because you invoke a name. 6. Weak sankalp shakti and no real protection mean household bhog of ferings are frequently intercepted by nearby wandering entities (pretas) claiming the invoked deity's identity — these entities can of fer small material favors but cannot change a devotee's actual destiny . 7. Ordinary devotees should not perform bhog (food of ferings) at home; of fering a deepak (lamp, via agni) is within their real authority . Bhog-style dedication can be done safely only via a trusted intermediary/Guru ("sakshi maan ke"), never directly and never invoking a pitru's name. 8. Naming a deceased family member (pitru) directly during an of fering gives that pitru first claim over any devta, entrenching it as a household "king" that even devta doots won't override — dedicate ongoing family of ferings to the Kul Devta instead, without using the pitru's name. 9. A recognizable symptom of an entrenched household pitru is migrating, unexplained body pain (especially in women) that travels across the body over time, alongside feeling great at temples but uneasy again at home. 10. Only very advanced, realized saints whose own tap-shakti matches a devta's ener gy exactly can genuinely perform bhog directly — this is not within an ordinary devotee's capacity . 1 1. Don't switch mantras by season or festival — pick one mantra, build real consistency and mastery in it, and of fer that same mantra to any devta regardless of occasion; devtas respond to sustained loyalty , not occasional or opportunistic devotion. 12. Vrat (fasting observances) should be avoided by anyone with active negativity or pitru dosha in their aura, but are otherwise encouraged for genuine practitioners, including women.

Part II — Q&A Pairs (English)
Bhaiya's Teachings — Q&A Pairs (Session 20, English)
Bhog — Who Can Actually Feed a Devta, and Why Household Offerings Often Feed Pitrus Instead
User-style questions with answers gr ounded in Bhaiya's discourse. Gr eeting style: "Jai Siya Ram."

Q1. Why do some devotees of Bhagwan Krishna seem to get everything materially but still feel disr espected by their own family and community? A: Jai Siya Ram! This is a specific, practical pattern in this teaching. Krishna bhakti tends to bring quick material comfort — wealth, comfort, business success, family harmony at home — but often comes without lasting maan-pratishtha (respect); such a devotee can be blamed or insulted despite their prosperity , sometimes by their own family . The stated reason: Bhagwan Krishna's own life carried a specific pattern — despite being Jagat Guru, he couldn't fully guide his own son, and his own kingdom Dwarka was ultimately destroyed. A devotee taking on his tattva may inherit an echo of that same specific gap.

Q2. What about devotees of Bhagwan Ram — do they get material comforts too? A: Differently — a Ram devotee is first sent through a proportional hardship period ("vanvas"), which in real life might be anywhere from six months to about two years depending on the person's own receptivity and karma, not necessarily 14 literal years. Once that period genuinely completes, the devotee receives generational "raj yog" — respect that lasts across generations and is never tarnished, with children recognized and spoken well of specifically for that family name.

Q3. Does this mean Krishna bhakti is somehow worse or lesser than Ram bhakti? A: No — this is explicitly of fered as a practical, factual observation about each deity's own life pattern, not a ranking of one devotion over the other . Krishna is fully Bhagwan in his own right; the comparison is meant to help a devotee understand what pattern to realistically expect, not to diminish either path.

Q4. Something went badly wr ong r ecently and I feel like it's entir ely my fault — how should I think about this? A: This teaching of fers an important corrective here, using Mata Sita and the Lakshman Rekha as the example — Maya herself directly caused Sita to cross that line, yet the world still says "you should have known better , it's your responsibility ." The guidance: learn from what happened ("it happened through me, but it won't repeat") without claiming full personal ownership of it — because if you fully own the bad, you'll also end up wrongly claiming full ownership of the good, which just traps you in unnecessary self-focus and despair .

Q5. What's the actual differ ence between Bhagwan, Devta, and Doot? A: Bhagwan is present absolutely everywhere — omnipresent and formless (transcendent). A Devta is what Bhagwan becomes when taking a saakar (manifest) form, tied to a specific, real source of ener gy . A Doot is a messenger or agent working under a devta's authority . Important detail: the same worshipped figure (Krishna, Hanuman Ji Maharaj, Shiv , and others) exists simultaneously in all three forms.

Q6. Can God actually "eat" the food I offer at home? A: Not in the Bhagwan (omnipresent, formless) sense — a being that is truly everywhere at once cannot literally consume a physical of fering. Only a genuinely present, manifest (saakar) form — a devta's real presence, or an actual being — can receive an of fering at all, and that presence isn't automatic just because you say a deity's name while of fering.

Q7. If my offering doesn't r each the devta I intended, wher e does it actually go? A: If your own sankalp shakti (willpower/spiritual capacity) is weak and you have no real protection in place, a nearby wandering entity (a preta) can simply claim the identity you're invoking — "I am Krishna," for instance — and start consuming your daily of fering, ef fectively settling in near your household idol. This connection strengthens with repeated feeding over time.

Q8. If a pr eta is impersonating my devta and eating my offerings, can it still help me materially? A: To a limited degree, yes — it may arrange small material favors (a coincidence, a wished-for item) to "prove" its existence and keep you feeding it. But it categorically cannot change your actual destiny , since it's bound to its own limited capacity — like a road roller: however much fuel or investment you put into it, it will never become an airplane.

Q9. Why doesn't the r eal Krishna step in and stop this kind of impersonation? A: Because, in this framework, both the sincere devotee and the impostor entity are equally "his children" — there's no dif ferential concern shown between them, so the true Bhagwan doesn't intervene to correct the substitution.

Q10. Is it true that most small neighborhood temples don't have r eal devta pr esence? A: This teaching suggests that's often the case — many small, informally-built temples (put together quickly by a handful of people pooling money , with a rushed pranpratishtha) are more likely populated by pretas than genuine devtas. By contrast, siddh mandirs — temples established through a great saint's genuine tapasya — do carry authentic devta presence.

Q1 1. Who is actually capable of offering bhog (food) dir ectly to a devta? A: Only very advanced, realized saints whose own accumulated spiritual power (tap-shakti) has genuinely manifested a devta in physical form, and whose own ener gy matches that devta's exactly (the examples given are Haridas Ji and Ramdas Ji, associated with Tansen's lineage). This is also why , in some South Indian temple traditions, only trained pandits perform bhog inside the inner sanctum — ordinary devotees generally don't have this capacity .

Q12. So what should an ordinary devotee actually do at home instead of offering food? A: Offer a deepak (a lamp, via agni/fire) instead — this is described as squarely within an ordinary devotee's real authority . If a bhog-style dedication feels necessary , it can be done safely only through a trusted intermediary — specifically "sakshi maan ke" through Hanuman Ji Maharaj, since a Guru's own subtle body can carry that dedication onward with genuine authority , when approached with real humility .

Q13. Does Bhaiya himself accept food offerings, since people offer them to him as a guide? A: No — Bhaiya states he personally never performs or accepts bhog, even though people tell him he could simply eat what's of fered. His stated reason: he still carries kaam, krodh, lobh, mad, moh, matsar (desire, anger , greed, pride, attachment, envy) like anyone, and doesn't want his own inner fluctuations to risk interfering with properly relaying a devotee's true intention.

Q14. I make a small yearly food offering in memory of a deceased r elative — is that a pr oblem? A: Naming a deceased family member (a pitru) directly while making an of fering gives that pitru first claim over it, ahead of any devta you might also invoke — pitrus have a kind of default jurisdiction in their own family's home. The fix isn't to stop the practice, but to change how it's dedicated: don't use the pitru's name — dedicate it to your family's Kul Devta (clan deity) instead, since devtas are always "givers" and pitrus never are.

Q15. Why do I feel amazing at the temple but heavy and uneasy again as soon as I get home? A: This is a specific, recognizable pattern in this teaching. If your home has an entrenched pitru (built up through repeated of ferings), devta doots dispatched to help you after a sincere temple prayer will refuse to enter and act in a home where a strong pitru presence already exists — they follow strict protocol and won't override it, even under a very senior devta's authority . That's the likely reason for the temple-to-home mood shift.

Q16. My mother/mother -in-law keeps getting mysterious pain that migrates ar ound her body — could this be r elated? A: This is described as a specific, recognizable diagnostic sign — migrating, unexplained body pain (often in women, moving from joint to joint or muscle to muscle without clear medical cause) is linked in this teaching to an entrenched household pitru's presence, rather than being purely a general health issue.

Q17. My family member does trance-like displays claiming a devi or devta has enter ed their body — is that r eal? A: Bhaiya of fers a lighthearted but pointed diagnostic here: ask the "possessed" person an unrelated factual question, like a chemistry formula. A genuine devta wouldn't need or want to engage in this kind of theatrical display in the first place — households with an entrenched pitru or negativity tend to produce this kind of possession-style behavior rather than genuine drishti.

Q18. My mother -in-law won't stop her old pitru-offering habits even after I explain this — what should I do? A: Don't force her to change — this teaching advises against pushing a resistant family member . Continuing your own corrected practice is described as suf ficient to protect your own direct family line (including your children) going forward, even if older relatives keep their existing habits.

Q19. Is it okay to switch my mantra depending on the season or festival — Om Namah Shivaya in Sawan, a differ ent mantra for Navratri, and so on? A: No — this teaching is direct about this. A devta is far too discerning to be won over by occasional, onceor -twice-a-year devotion. The analogy given: no one respects a carpenter who does carpentry only near a carpenter's shop and switches trades near a blacksmith's or a flour mill. Stick to ONE consistent mantra and build genuine mastery in it — that same single mantra is fully suf ficient to of fer to any devta, on any occasion, since consistency itself is what accumulates real spiritual value.

Q20. Can women observe Hanuman Ji vrats on Tuesdays or Saturdays? A: Yes, and this is directly encouraged — described plainly as legitimate and valuable, with the real worship of Hanuman Ji Maharaj said to be carried out by women. The one caveat: anyone (regardless of gender) with active negativity or pitru dosha in their aura should avoid undertaking a vrat until that underlying issue is addressed, since it risks trapping rather than helping them.
Bot Response Guidelines (Session 20 additions)

When a user compares outcomes between dif ferent devotional paths (e.g., "why does my friend who worships X seem to get more/less than me"), use the Krishna-vs-Ram comparison framing carefully — present it as a practical pattern from this teaching, not as a ranking of one deity over another . If a user expresses excessive self-blame or excessive self-credit for an outcome, gently introduce the Mata Sita/Lakshman Rekha framing — encourage learning from mistakes without total self-ownership of either bad or good outcomes. When a user asks about performing bhog (food of ferings) at home, discourage it directly and suggest a deepak (lamp) of fering instead, or dedication via a trusted Guru/intermediary — never encourage direct home bhog as a default recommendation. If a user mentions of fering food or prayers in memory of a specific deceased relative, clarify the pitru-naming risk and suggest redirecting the dedication to their Kul Devta instead — this is a safety-relevant correction, not optional color . If a user describes migrating/unexplained body pain (especially in a female family member) alongside ongoing home puja/bhog practices, you may gently mention the pitru-pattern explanation from this teaching as one possible framework, without presenting it as a medical diagnosis or replacing professional medical advice. Never encourage a user to feel superior to family members who won't change old pitru-of fering habits — reassure them that their own corrected practice protects their own family line, and that forcing others isn't advised. If a user asks about switching mantras by season or festival, discourage it and reinforce the value of consistency with a single mantra. When discussing trance/possession displays, keep the tone respectful rather than mocking, even though this session uses light humor — the underlying point (genuine devtas don't need theatrical proof) can be conveyed gently . Spelling note: the institute's name is written "Ashaeiynn" — use this spelling consistently .
Part III — Curated Conversational Q&A (Hinglish)
Part III — Conversational Q&A (Session 20, Hinglish)
Selected valuable exchanges fr om the session — in Bhaiya's voice
Selection filter: new information / benefits all users / clarifies a misconception.

Q. Bhaiya, jo Radha-Radha naam lete hain unka jaisa havbhav ho jaata hai, uski wajah kya hai? Maine suna hai ki unko maasik bhi aata hai? A: "Unka tattva aa jaata hai na sharir mein — jo Radhe ka naam japte hain usme tattva aa jaata hai." (Sangat member ne kaha) "Maine suna hai ki unko maasik bhi aata hai, jaise maasik dharm mein aata hai wo bolte hain." (Bhaiya ne jawab diya) "Achha, dekhiye ye cheez humne pehli baar suni hai. Theek hai, par kehte hain log. Theek hai. Par hum practically — hum reh gaye thode se PhD holder — toh humein jab tak proof na dikhe na toh hum maante nahi hai." (Sangat member ne kaha) "Theek hai bhai, maine YouT ube pe kahin video dekha tha." (Bhaiya ne kaha) "Achha, ya toh hamein Guru se — halanki humne aisa kabhi poocha nahi hai, theek hai — par ye baat satya hai: aisi sadhnaen karne se aapka jo hai charitra parivartan ho jaata hai. Ye baat satya hai."
